Circumstances of Worship
SUR-kum-stan-sez uhv WUR-ship
noun phrase (theological)
From Latin circumstantia, that which stands around; the surrounding details of worship ordered by prudence, as distinguished from the commanded elements.

📖 Biblical Definition

The circumstances of worship are the surrounding particulars of how the church gathers—time, place, posture, and order—which Scripture does not prescribe in detail but leaves to be ordered by Christian prudence and the light of nature, in distinction from the elements of worship, which Christ has positively commanded. The Westminster and Baptist Confessions teach that the whole counsel of God is set down in Scripture, yet add that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God and government of the church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. This is the heart of the regulative principle. The elements—reading and preaching the Word, prayer, singing, the sacraments, the giving of offerings—are fixed by divine command, and the church may neither add to them nor subtract from them. But whether the service begins at ten or eleven, whether the saints sit or stand, what building shelters them, how long the sermon runs—these Scripture does not command, and they fall under the wise ordering of the elders. The governing rule is Paul's, that all things be done decently and in order. The distinction guards two errors at once: it forbids the inventing of new elements that God never appointed, and it forbids the binding of consciences over indifferent details that God left free. Thus the church worships only as commanded, yet orders the unscripted particulars by sanctified wisdom for edification and peace.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Circumstances of worship are the unscripted particulars—time, place, order—ordered by prudence, as opposed to the commanded elements.

CIRCUMSTANCES OF WORSHIP, noun phrase. From Latin circumstantia, that which stands around.

The surrounding details of worship—time, place, posture, sequence—not prescribed in Scripture.

Matters ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence under the general rules of the Word.

Distinguished from elements, which are the parts of worship Christ has positively commanded.

The governing rule is: "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40).

📖 Key Scripture

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

1Co 14:26 — "How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying."

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Deu 12:32 — "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The distinction is the Reformed safeguard against both will-worship and the binding of consciences over indifferent things.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger here is older and recurring: the confusion of circumstances with elements. On one side, men invent new acts of worship—images, ceremonies, dramatic spectacles—and defend them as mere circumstance, when in truth they are unwarranted elements, the will-worship Paul condemns in Colossians 2:23. On the other, rigorists bind the conscience over genuinely indifferent particulars, treating the hour of service or the style of a building as though Scripture had commanded it.

The principle to recover is the precise distinction the Confessions draw: elements are fixed by divine command and may be neither added to nor diminished, while circumstances common to all human gatherings are ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence under the Word's general rules. This keeps worship pure, admitting only what Christ appointed, and keeps it free, refusing to enslave consciences over what God left open. Decently and in order is the standard—reverence without invention, order without tyranny.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on the regulative principle and Paul's rule of order in 1 Corinthians 14.

expand to see more

1 Corinthians 14:40 commands that all things be done decently and in order.

1 Corinthians 14:26 sets edification as the aim of the gathered assembly.

Colossians 2:23 condemns will-worship—invented elements with a mere show of wisdom.

Deuteronomy 12:32 forbids adding to or diminishing from what God commands in worship.

WCF 1.6 and 1689 1.6 distinguish commanded elements from prudently ordered circumstances.

Usage

"Used of unscripted details: "the hour of worship is a circumstance, not an element.""

"Used in defense of order: "circumstances are ordered by Christian prudence.""

"Used to guard purity: "new elements cannot be smuggled in as circumstances.""
